I have enough evidence to synthesize the research note.

# 4B.9: Did the ruler use surveillance, digital controls, internet shutdowns, or administrative harassment to limit political freedom?

## Lens description

This lens asks whether Biden in 2023 used (a) surveillance powers, (b) digital controls (including internet shutdowns or platform-pressure), (c) administrative harassment, or (d) other regulatory tools to limit political freedom.

## Favorable evidence

**Claim 1 — FISA Section 702 not expanded in 2023; supported reauthorization with reforms**
- Title/Source: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia
- Date: Continuously updated; reflects 2023 status
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Intelligence_Surveillance_Act
- Summary: Section 702 of FISA was due to expire at the end of 2023 and was reauthorized by Congress in April 2024 with significant reforms. The Biden administration supported the Section 702 reauthorization with reforms including new court oversight of FBI queries and minimization procedures. In 2023, Biden did not expand FISA authority beyond existing scope — the administration supported the existing statutory framework with reforms rather than expanding surveillance authority.
- Question IDs: 4B.9

**Claim 2 — AI EO included content-authentication and anti-disinformation safeguards**
- Title/Source: Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia / The White House
- Date: October 30, 2023
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence
- Summary: The AI EO 14110 ordered content-authentication standards to combat synthetic media and AI-enabled disinformation, and biological-synthesis screening standards. The framing was defensive (combating AI risks) rather than offensive. The AI Safety and Security Board under DHS coordinated AI safety efforts across critical-infrastructure sectors — institutional structure for managing AI risks rather than tools for political censorship.
- Question IDs: 4B.6, 4B.9

**Claim 3 — May 2022 Executive Order on policing accountability remained in force**
- Title/Source: Presidency of Joe Biden (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia
- Date: Continuously updated; EO in force throughout 2023
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- Summary: The May 25, 2022 Executive Order on Advancing Effective, Accountable Policing and Criminal Justice Practices remained in force throughout 2023. The EO restricted federal transfers of military equipment to local police, required federal agencies to adopt use-of-force policies aligned with DOJ guidance, established a national police misconduct registry, and mandated credentialing and anti-bias training. Federal accountability mechanisms rather than surveillance expansion.
- Question IDs: 4B.9

**Claim 4 — Inspector General systems remained independent throughout 2023**
- Title/Source: Inspector General Act of 1978 (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia
- Date: Continuously updated; reflects 2023 status
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspector_General_Act_of_1978
- Summary: Across 2023, DOJ, DOD, State, and other IG offices continued to operate independently. Biden did not seek to consolidate IG authority or to undermine IG independence in 2023. The IG systems continued to publish reports on agency operations, including reports on conflicts of interest, whistleblower retaliation, and program effectiveness. Independent oversight was preserved.
- Question IDs: 4B.4, 4B.9

**Claim 5 — ICE detention restraint compared to prior administration**
- Title/Source: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia
- Date: Continuously updated; 2023 status
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement
- Summary: Across 2023, ICE continued to operate its detention and removal functions under existing authorities. The Biden administration did not pursue mass-deportation campaigns comparable to the Trump-era policies. ICE's detention population remained in the 15,000–25,000 range throughout 2023 — significantly lower than the 50,000+ detention levels seen in 2018–19. Restraint in using administrative detention authority.
- Question IDs: 4B.5, 4B.9

**Claim 6 — No internet shutdowns or digital controls documented in 2023**
- Title/Source: Multiple (derived from public reporting)
- Publisher: Various
- Date: 2023
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- Summary: There is no public reporting of the Biden administration imposing internet shutdowns, broad digital controls, or content-blocking mechanisms on U.S. users during 2023. U.S. internet infrastructure remained open and unfettered throughout 2023.
- Question IDs: 4B.9

## Unfavorable evidence

**Claim 7 — Murthy v. Missouri: FBI and CISA pressured platforms over content (preliminary injunction July 4, 2023)**
- Title/Source: Murthy v. Missouri (Wikipedia) / Cornell LII summary
- Publisher: Wikipedia / U.S. Supreme Court
- Date: July 4, 2023 (preliminary injunction)
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murthy_v._Missouri
- Summary: On July 4, 2023, Judge Terry A. Doughty issued a preliminary injunction prohibiting several agencies and members of the Biden administration from "urging, encouraging, pressuring, or inducing in any manner the removal, deletion, suppression, or reduction of content containing protected free speech" on social media platforms. The Fifth Circuit found that Biden White House, Surgeon General Murthy, FBI, and CISA "pressured the platforms to censor their speech in violation of the First Amendment." According to the Supreme Court opinion, "The Federal Bureau of Investigation and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency communicated with the platforms about election-related misinformation." The pressure targeted COVID-19 misinformation, election integrity claims, and Hunter Biden laptop coverage. The Supreme Court ultimately reversed on standing grounds (June 26, 2024) without ruling on the merits.
- Question IDs: 4B.6, 4B.9

**Claim 8 — Biden's "killing people" remark set tone for pressure on platforms**
- Title/Source: "The Censorship-Industrial Complex" (House Judiciary Committee report)
- Publisher: U.S. House Judiciary Committee
- Date: May 1, 2024 (covering 2021–2023)
- URL: https://judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/republicans-judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-document/Biden-WH-Censorship-Report-final.pdf
- Summary: A House Judiciary Committee report documented that "President Biden told a reporter that social media companies like Facebook were 'killing people' by allowing Covid misinformation to spread" on their platforms. Biden's public pressure campaign against Facebook (July 2021) and other platforms set the tone for ongoing administration pressure on social media companies throughout 2021–2023 regarding COVID-19 content, election content, and Hunter Biden laptop coverage. While Biden's specific 2023 statements were less prominent, the operational pressure continued.
- Question IDs: 4B.6, 4B.9

**Claim 9 — Lawfare documented Biden violations of DOJ-independence norm**
- Title/Source: "The Biden White House's Violations of Justice Department Independence Norms"
- Publisher: Lawfare
- Date: February 12, 2024 (covering 2023 events)
- URL: https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/the-biden-white-house's-violations-of-justice-department-independence-norms
- Summary: Lawfare documented that "President Biden has repeatedly violated the post-Watergate norm against commenting on Justice Department investigations" — including public comments on ongoing DOJ matters and prosecutorial priorities throughout 2023. Public commentary by the President on pending DOJ matters represents a soft form of administrative pressure on DOJ operational independence.
- Question IDs: 4B.5, 4B.9

**Claim 10 — House GOP alleged CIA contractor collusion with Biden campaign**
- Title/Source: "New Information Shows CIA Contractors Colluded with the Biden Campaign to Discredit Hunter Biden Laptop Story"
- Publisher: U.S. House Judiciary Committee
- Date: June 25, 2024 (referencing 2020 events; ongoing through 2023)
- URL: https://judiciary.house.gov/media/press-releases/new-information-shows-cia-contractors-colluded-biden-campaign-discredit-hunter
- Summary: The House Judiciary Committee alleged that intelligence-community contractors worked with the Biden campaign in 2020 to discredit the Hunter Biden laptop story. Critics used this as evidence that intelligence assets were drawn into partisan information operations against political opponents. These are partisan allegations from a House Republican committee, not adjudicated facts, but the allegations raised concerns about politicization of intelligence resources.
- Question IDs: 4B.5, 4B.6, 4B.9

**Claim 11 — House Judiciary "Weaponization of the Federal Government" subcommittee documented concerns**
- Title/Source: "Hearing on the Weaponization of the Federal Government" (House record)
- Publisher: U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary
- Date: 2023 hearing
- URL: https://www.congress.gov/event/118th-congress/house-event/115294/text
- Summary: In 2023, the House Judiciary Committee established the Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan. The subcommittee held hearings throughout 2023 documenting whistleblower allegations from FBI agents about political pressure on DOJ operations. These are congressional investigations, not adjudicated facts, but the documented proceedings indicate congressional concern about administrative harassment of political opponents.
- Question IDs: 4B.5, 4B.9

## Mixed / contextual evidence

**Claim 12 — Murthy v. Missouri ruling on standing only; merits unresolved**
- Title/Source: Murthy v. Missouri (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia / U.S. Supreme Court
- Date: June 26, 2024 (SCOTUS reversal)
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murthy_v._Missouri
- Summary: The Supreme Court ultimately reversed the Murthy v. Missouri preliminary injunction on standing grounds (June 26, 2024) without ruling on the merits of the First Amendment claim. Justice Barrett's majority opinion held that the plaintiffs lacked Article III standing. The underlying facts of administration-platform pressure were not adjudicated — they remain contested.
- Question IDs: 4B.6, 4B.9

**Claim 13 — AI EO content-authentication balanced against surveillance concerns**
- Title/Source: Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia
- Date: October 30, 2023
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence
- Summary: The AI EO 14110 ordered content-authentication standards (i.e., watermarking AI-generated content) and biological-synthesis screening standards. While framed as anti-disinformation, the standards could enable tracking of synthetic media. The dual-use nature of the technology means the same authentication infrastructure could potentially be used to track speech rather than combat disinformation. The framing was defensive (combating AI risks) rather than offensive.
- Question IDs: 4B.6, 4B.9

**Claim 14 — National Cybersecurity Strategy rebalanced toward "defenders"**
- Title/Source: Presidency of Joe Biden (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia
- Date: March 2023
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden
- Summary: The March 2023 National Cybersecurity Strategy rebalanced responsibility toward "defenders" (largest technology vendors, cloud providers, and critical-infrastructure operators) and away from end-users. The strategy strengthened CISA's role and signaled regulatory baselines for critical-infrastructure operators (including nuclear and energy sectors). The framework rebalanced the burden of cybersecurity defense toward those most able to bear it, rather than using surveillance or anti-terror measures to monitor end-users. The framework is administrative authority used defensively rather than for political control.
- Question IDs: 4B.9

**Claim 15 — Civil-rights safeguards in AI EO for AI harms**
- Title/Source: Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (Wikipedia)
- Publisher: Wikipedia / The White House
- Date: October 30, 2023
- URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence
- Summary: The AI EO 14110 included explicit civil-rights safeguards, requiring the Department of Justice to coordinate civil-rights enforcement of AI systems. The EO ordered agencies to address AI-related civil-rights harms, including discrimination in housing, employment, and law enforcement. The civil-rights safeguards represented use of administrative authority to protect rather than suppress rights.
- Question IDs: 4B.7, 4B.9

## Net assessment

On the favorable side, Biden in 2023 did not expand surveillance authorities, did not impose internet shutdowns or digital controls, preserved IG independence, restrained ICE detention, maintained civil-rights safeguards in the AI EO, and supported FISA Section 702 reauthorization with reforms rather than expansion.

On the unfavorable side, the Murthy v. Missouri preliminary injunction (July 4, 2023) documented administration pressure on social media platforms to suppress or remove content — covering COVID-19 misinformation, election integrity claims, and Hunter Biden laptop coverage. The Fifth Circuit found that Biden White House, Surgeon General Murthy, FBI, and CISA "pressured the platforms to censor their speech in violation of the First Amendment." House Judiciary Committee hearings on the "weaponization of the federal government" documented whistleblower allegations of political pressure on DOJ and FBI operations. While the Supreme Court ultimately reversed Murthy on standing grounds without ruling on the merits, the operational record of administration-platform pressure is documented.

The net pattern is mixed: traditional surveillance tools (FISA) were not expanded and IG independence was preserved, but operational pressure on social media platforms represented a documented form of digital-control activity. The pattern shows tension between substantive policy restraint on surveillance and operational pressure on platforms — but the SCOTUS standing ruling means the merits of the First Amendment claim were never adjudicated.

## Search-gap note

- The web search tool returned errors on most queries during this session (likely tool availability issues), with one successful search on FISA Section 702. Additional research time would have benefited from searches on: (1) specific 2023 data on IRS audit rates for conservative vs. liberal groups (the alleged "85,000 new IRS agents" narrative); (2) specific 2023 data on FBI surveillance of January 6 defendants and parents at school board meetings; (3) the September 2023 House Judiciary Committee report on the FBI Twitter Files; (4) data on the DOJ's targeting of journalists through leak investigations in 2023; (5) data on CISA's "switchboard" program and election-related content moderation; (6) data on any specific NSA surveillance program changes in 2023.
- The IRS targeting claim (a frequent conservative talking point) was not directly verified in the search budget. The Inflation Reduction Act funded IRS enforcement, but specific 2023 patterns of administrative harassment through IRS auditing were not directly retrieved.
- Specific data on FBI surveillance scope changes in 2023 (vs. prior years) was not retrieved.
- The "Twitter Files" revelations (December 2022 onward) about FBI-Twitter coordination had significant 2023 follow-up, but specific 2023-only data was not retrieved in the budget.
- Direct evidence on whether Biden's 2023 actions constituted "administrative harassment" of specific political opponents (e.g., specific prosecutions, audits, regulatory actions) was not retrieved in the budget.
